1:
The king’s age sets a chronological problem solved two ways. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) works it out: twenty at his accession and sixteen years on the throne make him thirty-six at death, yet Hezekiah succeeded at twenty-five, so Ahaz fathered him at eleven. He rejects as a violent solution the rendering that Ahaz was twenty when his father began to reign, preferring the text as it stands and a father of eleven or twelve, since in eastern countries the young are marriageable at ten or twelve. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) mends the number instead, holding it should probably be twenty-five with the Greek, Syriac and Arabic of the parallel in Chronicles, since otherwise Ahaz was begotten when his father was ten or eleven, a thing perhaps not impossible in the East.

On the reign itself they differ in scale. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) makes it a study in degeneracy: few and evil were his days, evil because he had none of that concern for the instituted worship of God for which David was celebrated. That he held the throne by God’s covenant with David only aggravated the wickedness, for a good extraction is a disgrace to him who degenerates from it. He walked in their way unprompted, joined to the kings of Israel by no affinity as Jehoram was to the house of Ahab, and where they could at least plead policy for their idolatry he had no such pretence. John Gill (reformed) adds that the calf-worship ran against both his education and his political interest, the one thing that had swayed the kings of Israel. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) set it in a longer development: under Uzziah and Jotham increasing wealth had bred luxury and self-security among the upper classes, and under Ahaz these grew into open apostasy, until he shut the doors of the porch and suspended the temple worship altogether.

Whether the son was actually burnt is disputed. John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) says flatly that the passing was by way of oblation, to be consumed for a burnt-offering, the practice of the heathen and of some Israelites after them. Ellicott agrees that the chronicler rightly explains it as a sacrifice by fire, suggesting with Movers that the phrase may have arisen from the idea of burning as a passage to union with the deity, or may be a mere euphemism; he reckons Ahaz the first Israelite king to offer such a sacrifice, a last desperate resource against his northern enemies, and calls it absurd to suppose with Thenius that he meant it in love to his child. Henry alone leaves room for something less: he burnt some of them, as Chronicles says expressly, and perhaps made others pass between two fires in token of their dedication to the idol, Hezekiah himself not excepted, though he was afterwards never the worse for it.

The high places are read for geography and blame. Ellicott observes that they are distinguished from the hills, two different prepositions being used in the Hebrew as in the English, and that a high place was a local sanctuary; on the green tree he reports Thenius that a thick-foliaged and shadow-yielding rather than a merely green tree is meant, quoting the prophet on burning incense under oaks and poplars because the shadow thereof is good. Gill marks the innovation: no king of Judah before him had done this, his predecessors conniving at the practice without their own example. Henry turns it on the father: had Jotham only had zeal enough to take the high places away, his sons might not have been debauched, for those who connive at sin know not what dangerous snares they lay for those who come after them. Ahaz chose hills for the prospect and green trees for the shade, a religion little worth, guided by fancy and not by faith.
5:
The allies’ aim and failure get political and providential readings. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) notes that the verse agrees almost word for word with the opening of the prophecy in Isaiah, and that the confederates meant to force Judah into their revolt against Assyria, judging the surest way to be the dethroning of David’s dynasty for a creature of their own; the words could not overcome him are literally that they were not able to war, the allies unable to storm a city Uzziah and Jotham had strongly fortified. John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) credits the failure to God, who of his own mere grace undertook his protection and disappointed his enemies’ hopes, while John Gill (reformed) makes God the mover of the attack, the kings coming up moved to it by the Lord to chastise Ahaz for his idolatry.

Whether Elath fell to Syria or Edom turns on two similar Hebrew words. Ellicott sets out the case: the words for Syria and Edom are much alike in Hebrew writing, and the Hebrew margin, many manuscripts, the Greek and the Vulgate all read Edomites here, so that many critics would restore Edom throughout, making the sense that Rezin freed the Edomites from Uzziah’s yoke to win their co-operation; others keep the ordinary text, on which he simply expelled the Jews and planted a colony of Syrians. Gill traces the port from Edom to David and back at Joram’s revolt, then refuses the emendation outright, since it means substituting Edom for Aram, which Le Clerc has ventured without any authority. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) draws a moral from the loss: what can those keep who have lost their religion, and let them expect to be always on the losing hand.

On the embassy to Assyria the severest judgment is Henry’s, and Wesley repeats it in brief. Having forsaken God, Ahaz had neither courage nor strength to make head against his enemies, nor could he with any boldness ask help of God; those whose hearts condemn them will go anywhere in distress rather than to him. Was it because there was not a God in Israel that he sent to the Assyrian for help? The sin was its own punishment, for though he gained his point he made a bad bargain, enslaving himself in the words I am thy servant and thy son, when had he humbled himself so to God he might have been delivered on easier terms and needed only to part with his sins; and he impoverished himself besides, squeezing church and state to gratify his new patron. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) put the same act textually: Ahaz turned to Tiglath-pileser regarding neither the word of Isaiah which promised him salvation nor the prophet’s warning against an Assyrian alliance.

What the help was worth, and where the captives went, divide them. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) weighs it by the parallel, that this king distressed and strengthened him not: he took Damascus and slew Rezin, but gave no help against the Philistines and no forces against Israel, and took the royal and temple treasures, helping a little but distressing him on the whole. Ellicott turns to the monuments, where Damascus stands a two years’ siege and the earlier expedition is aimed at Pekah, who saved himself by instant submission; an inscription of the seventeenth year lists tribute from Jahuhazi of Judah, that is Ahaz, dating his submission. On Kir the two part company. Keil and Delitzsch take it for a district by the river Kur, which rises in Armenia, joins the Araxes and falls into the Caspian, though the river’s length makes the place impossible to fix. Ellicott reports that identification only to reject it, since Delitzsch objects that the one name cannot be the other and the Assyrian empire never reached that river, so that Kir must be sought in Mesopotamia.
10:
Why the altar took his fancy divides them. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) holds that the words for fashion and pattern and workmanship indicate an interest artistic rather than religious, and quotes Robertson Smith on a trifling and superstitious virtuoso who came home from a national crisis with his head full of curiosities. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) will have none of it: that Ahaz did this for an idolatrous purpose is evident from the parallel, where he sacrificed to the gods of Damascus because the gods of the kings of Syria helped them. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) takes both at once, supposing he saw it either while viewing the rarities of the place or while joining in their devotions, since there he thought it no harm to do as they did. It pleased his fancy extremely, being curiously carved where the altar he was trained up at was plain, so that Solomon had but a dull fancy beside the ingenious artist who made this one.

Urijah is judged twice over, and not alike. Henry prosecutes him: without dispute or objection he put the work in hand, prostituting his authority and betraying a trust that bound him to witness against all innovations. John Gill (reformed) is shorter: he built exactly to the figure sent him, against a command fixing both the form and matter of God’s altar, of which as high priest he could not be ignorant; he was a timeserver courting his prince, and it was like king like priest, both apostates. Ellicott, needing him for another purpose, notes only that this high priest appears to be the credible witness of the prophecy, his position securing his credit.

To whom the sacrifice went is the sharpest division, and Ellicott stands alone. He judges that nothing in this narrative tells against Ahaz having offered to Jehovah, that the Chronicles account must mean other sacrifices of his, and that like most of his contemporaries he thought the worship of Jehovah not incompatible with foreign cults. Against him Henry says the sacrifices went not to the God of Israel but to the gods of Damascus, and that having borrowed the Syrians’ altar it was no marvel he borrowed their gods. John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) is flatter still, that the offering went not to God but to the Syrian idols to whom that altar was appropriated, though he allows Ahaz may not yet have utterly forsaken God but worshipped idols alongside him. Ellicott adds a point none disputes: every version but one reads that the king went up upon the altar, so that Ahaz, like Uzziah, personally exercised the priestly function.

The displacing of the old altar is read as gradual encroachment. Ellicott notes that Urijah seems to have pushed the brasen altar nearer the sanctuary and set the Syrian one in its place, and that Ahaz, unsatisfied with an arrangement seeming to favour the old, drew it back to the north side of his own. Henry marks the progress: the invention at first jostled with God’s institution and at length jostled it out, for those will soon come to make nothing of God who will not make him their all. On the words reserving the brasen altar the readings multiply. Henry takes them for an oracle, observing that the altar was never designed for one, and reports the alternative that Ahaz meant only to consider what to do with it, the Jews saying its brass became his famous dial. Wesley follows him, reserving the use to the king, who might enquire God’s will by sacrifices joined with prayer, while Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) give that same sense of a thing about which he would consider. Ellicott allows consulting God with Rashi, or a thing to think about, or simply something to look at, and rejects two conjectures resting on a transposed verb and on the Syriac.
17:
The stripping of the furniture is described closely and read for motive. John Gill (reformed) explains that the ten lavers in which the priests washed stood on brazen bases whose borders carried figures of lions and oxen and cherubim, and that Ahaz cut these off either to deface them in contempt or to convert the brass to other uses. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) list the acts — the carved panels of the stands broken off, every basin removed, the brazen sea taken down from the brazen oxen and set on a pedestal built of stones rather than the court pavement — then say plainly that the reason he mutilated these sacred vessels is not given. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) supplies one: these were the vessels the priests washed in, so against them he seems to have had a particular spite, it being one of the greatest prejudices that can be done to religion to obstruct the purifying of the Lord’s ministers.

The covert for the sabbath defeats all of them, and they say so. John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) states outright that its form and use are now unknown, and reports it generally understood of some building: where the priests whose weekly course had ended waited for the next; or where the temple guard kept station; or where the king sat to hear God’s word and see the sacrifices. Gill inclines to the last, suggesting the cover of the royal scaffold, perhaps of rich cloth of gold. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) notes a great number of conjectures and adds one from Jarchi, that it was a covert way by which the kings of Judah reached the temple, removed lest the Assyrian going along it should see the sacred vessels and covet them. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) calls the expression very obscure and settles for the covered hall set apart for the king on holy days, a reading the Vulgate and the Syriac attest.

What was done to it, and for whom, divides the two schools directly. Ellicott offers as an alternative rendering that Ahaz altered these places in the house of the Lord, stripping them of their ornamental work — the very reading Keil and Delitzsch, ascribing it to Ewald and Thenius, dismiss as quite arbitrary. Ellicott also presses the preposition, reading not for the king of Assyria but from fear of him, since Ahaz durst not appear before Tiglath without a present. Henry supposes the visit actually paid, the Assyrian finding fault with the royal entry as an inconvenience and a disparagement to his palace; Clarke sees the communication between palace and temple cut, so that his overlord should not enter by the passage to which the priests alone had access.

The verdict on the reign is unanimous, the burial read as its seal. Henry has him resign his life in the midst of his days at thirty-six leaving the kingdom to a better man, Hezekiah proving as much a friend to the temple as his father had been an enemy — and perhaps this was the very son he had made to pass through the fire, but God by his grace snatched him as a brand out of the burning. Gill and Keil and Delitzsch agree he was buried in the city of David but not in the sepulchres of the kings, which Gill ascribes to his wickedness and Clarke calls undoubtedly a mark of degradation. Clarke closes hardest: the reign was disastrous because impious, a scourge and not a blessing, so that no worse king had yet sat on that throne — and this though he had for counsellor one of the greatest men the nation produced, and though God interposed for him against the two kings cut off as the prophet predicted. He had sufficient warning and was without excuse; he would sin, and therefore he must suffer.
